headline: Man's meat-only "lion diet" claims 90% psoriasis cure, sparks health-tech frenzy.
subheadline: While a single steak may have cleared skin, governments are carving up children's digital lives and borders alike.
editorialBody: Jared Kline, a 42‑year‑old welder from Bismarck, North Dakota, posted a grainy video on Thursday showing a scar‑free forearm. He swore the all‑meat regimen—dubbed the “lion diet”—erased 90 % of the psoriasis that had tormented him for two decades and lifted a depression that kept his kids from school. The diet costs him roughly $250 a week in premium cuts, a sum he claims is “cheaper than my old meds.” The internet cheered, the skeptics sneered, and the market barely flinched.

Across the continent, the EU is doing the opposite of a steak‑only cure: it wants to sever children from their digital crutches. Wired reported that EU regulators are drafting legislation to “break up kids and their chatbots,” effectively forcing developers to dismantle AI companions for users under 13. The BBC followed with a plan to restrict all social‑media access for under‑15s, citing mental‑health data that 27 % of teens experience anxiety linked to endless scrolling. The irony is palpable—while a man in the heartland claims salvation through carnivorous excess, Brussels is planning a digital fast‑track for the next generation.

The policy push is not merely paternalistic. TASS disclosed that Russia will open polling stations on its borders with the Baltic states and Poland, a move designed to capture expatriate votes for the Duma. Meanwhile, the same outlet noted Lavrov’s warning of a “massive wave of propaganda from the West” ahead of Russia’s elections. In the West, Wired flagged that hundreds of election deniers will appear on November ballots, a clear sign that democratic machinery is being weaponised from both sides. The juxtaposition of a personal health miracle and the grand‑scale manipulation of civic identity underscores a world where the body politic is being dissected as meticulously as a steak.

On the trading floor, the drama plays out in code. Solana (SOL) hovered at $97.81, its RSI at 61.0, MACD histogram a modest +0.1053, and Bollinger %B flirting at 0.89—technical candles that would normally spark a buying spree. Yet the Council’s own analysis warned of a fragile strength rating of just 0.33, neutral Fear & Greed at 51, and no news catalyst to justify the rally. Bitcoin’s sentiment sits at 65, Ethereum at 56, both buoyed by a 51‑53 market signal, but the underlying conviction is thin. In other words, the market is as hungry for direction as a cat eyeing a steak, yet the kitchen is empty.

The hunger extends beyond assets. NPR highlighted that pressure on global chokepoints is diverting Asian cargo to Arctic trade routes, a shift that could reshape freight economics before winter. Simultaneously, Rest of World reported South Africa’s bold stand against American data‑center expansion, insisting on sovereign cloud infrastructure. These moves hint at a re‑routing of both physical and digital flows, a quiet rebellion against the hegemony of Western logistics and data.

Asia’s own tremors are no less pronounced. SCMP warned that a record influx of university graduates has pushed China’s youth unemployment to 18.9 %, a demographic tinderbox that could fuel unrest. Hong Kong’s property market found a brief reprieve in lower rates, but the underlying precariousness remains, echoing Uganda’s recent reserve‑ratio hike to protect the shilling—a defensive move that mirrors the West’s own tightening grip on markets.

All this unfolds to the soundtrack of Packaging’s “Full Performance (Live on KEXP).” The raw, unpolished guitars feel like a barroom confession—gritty, immediate, and unapologetically honest, much like Kline’s steak‑laden testimony. The day’s video picks—DW’s live feed of Trump’s emergency declaration and BBC’s piece on a new “silicon species” of AI—add a cinematic backdrop to a world where reality and spectacle bleed together.

Sentiment scores paint a paradox: AI optimism at 64, elections at 68, yet conflict sits at a lukewarm 48. The public feels hopeful about tech’s promise while remaining wary of the guns and polls that still dominate headlines. This bifurcation is the undercurrent of every story we cover.

Looking ahead, the EU’s child‑AI legislation will be debated in the European Parliament next Tuesday, with a vote slated for September 25. Russia’s border polling stations must be operational by October 1. Solana’s next technical test will be the 50‑day moving average breach on October 5; a failure could see the bullish momentum evaporate. The Arctic shipping season opens officially on November 1, and China’s graduate cohort for 2026 is set to enter the job market in December, potentially inflating that 18.9 % unemployment figure.

The world is cutting meat, cutting code, cutting borders—each slice a reminder that someone always pays the price. If you’re tired of watching the same headlines repackaged, consider a subscription; the stories you fund keep the knives from getting dull.
